trap_notes.b: The Berlin Airlift happened in 1948–1949 during the Cold War.
trap_notes.c: Brest-Litovsk (1918) took Russia out of WWI after the U.S. had already entered.
trap_notes.d: The Munich Pact was a 1938 appeasement agreement before WWII.
trap_notes.default: Germany's 1917 Zimmermann Telegram proposed a German-Mexican alliance against the U.S.

prompt: Why did Congress reject FDR's 1937 'court-packing' plan to add new Supreme Court justices?

options.text: Lawmakers feared it would break checks and balances
The Constitution forbids Congress from setting Court size
All nine justices resigned before the vote took place
The Court had already approved every New Deal law

explanation: Even many Democrats opposed FDR's plan because expanding the Court to flip rulings threatened judicial independence.
fun_fact: Soon after, the Court began upholding key New Deal laws like Social Security and the Wagner Act anyway.

trap_notes.b: Congress does set the number of justices by law; the objection was political interference.
trap_notes.c: The justices did not resign; the Senate simply voted down the bill.
trap_notes.d: The Court had struck down major New Deal laws like the NIRA and AAA in 1935–1936.
trap_notes.default: Expanding the Court for political rulings was seen as violating separation of powers.

prompt: How did the 1941 Lend-Lease Act change U.S. policy before Pearl Harbor?

options.text: It let the U.S. supply Allies without demanding upfront cash
It banned all U.S. weapon sales to Britain and China
It sent two million U.S. soldiers to France in 1940
It required European buyers to haul goods on their own ships

explanation: Lend-Lease ended strict neutrality by letting the president lend or lease war supplies to countries vital to U.S. defense.
fun_fact: FDR compared Lend-Lease to lending a garden hose to a neighbor whose house was on fire.

trap_notes.b: Earlier 1930s Neutrality Acts banned weapon sales; Lend-Lease opened the supply tap.
trap_notes.c: U.S. combat troops did not enter Europe until after Pearl Harbor in late 1941.
trap_notes.d: Cash-and-carry (1939) required upfront cash and foreign ships; Lend-Lease removed cash barriers.
trap_notes.default: Lend-Lease supplied Britain, the USSR, and China on credit before the U.S. entered WWII.

prompt: What human farming practice combined with 1930s drought to create the Dust Bowl?

options.text: Plowing up deep-rooted prairie grass for wheat
Flooding Great Plains fields with river dams
Planting thick shelterbelts of trees across Kansas
Leaving all Plains grasslands untouched by tractors

explanation: Tractors tore up native prairie sod that held soil in place, so drought winds blew millions of tons of dry topsoil away.
fun_fact: New Deal agencies later taught contour plowing and planted millions of trees as windbreaks.

trap_notes.b: The region suffered severe drought, not river flooding.
trap_notes.c: Tree shelterbelts were a New Deal solution, not the cause of the Dust Bowl.
trap_notes.d: Heavy tractor plowing removed the protective native grass.
trap_notes.default: Removing native prairie grass left dry soil exposed to high Plains winds.

prompt: What constitutional principle did Brown v. Board of Education (1954) establish for public schools?

options.text: Separate schools are inherently unequal under the 14th Amendment
States may segregate schools if buildings match in cost
Only private schools are covered by the Equal Protection Clause
Local school boards outrank federal constitutional rulings

explanation: A unanimous Supreme Court overturned Plessy in public education, ruling that segregated schools violate the 14th Amendment.
fun_fact: NAACP attorney Thurgood Marshall argued the case and later became the first Black Supreme Court justice.

trap_notes.b: That was the old Plessy rule, which Brown explicitly rejected in education.
trap_notes.c: The 14th Amendment applies to state-run public schools.
trap_notes.d: Under the Supremacy Clause, federal constitutional rulings override state segregation laws.
trap_notes.default: Brown v. Board ruled that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.'

prompt: Why did Congress pass the 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act and 1914 Clayton Antitrust Act?

options.text: To break up monopolies and protect market competition
To guarantee every industry a single legal trust
To ban labor unions from collective bargaining
To nationalize all U.S. banks and steel mills

explanation: Antitrust laws targeted trusts that stifled competition and fixed prices, while the Clayton Act also protected peaceful union strikes.
fun_fact: The Supreme Court used the Sherman Act in 1911 to break Rockefeller's Standard Oil into 34 separate companies.

trap_notes.b: Antitrust laws aimed to stop monopolies, not protect them.
trap_notes.c: The 1914 Clayton Act actually exempted labor unions from antitrust prosecution.
trap_notes.d: The U.S. regulated private monopolies rather than taking over banks or steel.
trap_notes.default: Antitrust laws preserve competition when one trust dominates a market.

prompt: What First Amendment rule did Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) affirm during the Vietnam War?

options.text: Students keep free-speech rights unless speech disrupts class
Principals may ban any political symbols at school
First Amendment rights apply only to adults off campus
Only spoken speeches count as protected expression

explanation: Students wore black armbands to protest Vietnam, and the Court ruled students keep free-speech rights at school.
fun_fact: Mary Beth Tinker was just 13 years old when she wore the black armband to her junior high school.

trap_notes.b: Schools cannot ban peaceful political expression just because administrators disagree with it.
trap_notes.c: The Court specifically protected students inside public schools.
trap_notes.d: Wearing symbolic armbands was protected as symbolic speech.
trap_notes.default: Tinker protected peaceful student symbolic speech unless it causes substantial disruption.

prompt: What Cold War strategy guided the 1947 Truman Doctrine of aid to Greece and Turkey?

options.text: Containment to stop Soviet communism from spreading
Isolationism to withdraw from all European affairs
Appeasement to grant new territory to Moscow
Mercantilism to tax European raw-material exports

explanation: Based on George Kennan's containment idea, Truman pledged U.S. support to free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressure.
fun_fact: Congress approved $400 million in emergency aid to Greece and Turkey within two months of Truman's speech.

trap_notes.b: The Truman Doctrine marked the end of traditional U.S. peacetime isolationism.
trap_notes.c: Appeasement was Britain and France's 1938 policy toward Hitler, not Truman's policy.
trap_notes.d: Mercantilism was an 18th-century colonial trade system.
trap_notes.default: Containment aimed to block Soviet expansion without starting World War III.

prompt: How did the 1956 Federal-Aid Highway Act reshape U.S. geography and commerce?

options.text: It sped up trucking, suburbs, and car travel nationwide
It replaced all freight railroads with local canals
It restricted interstate highways to East Coast cities
It slowed suburban growth by banning gas stations

explanation: Funded for national defense and commerce, the 41,000-mile Interstate network boosted trucking, suburbs, and cross-country travel.
fun_fact: As a young army officer in 1919, Dwight Eisenhower took 62 days to cross the U.S. by convoy, inspiring his 1956 highway push.

trap_notes.b: Highways boosted trucking rather than building canals.
trap_notes.c: The Interstate system connected major cities from coast to coast.
trap_notes.d: Highways accelerated suburban sprawl and roadside businesses.
trap_notes.default: Interstate highways transformed both suburban commuting and long-distance freight.

prompt: Which colonial grievance directly inspired the Fourth Amendment's ban on unreasonable searches?

options.text: British writs of assistance allowing blanket home searches
The Stamp Act fee on colonial marriage licenses
Parliament's tea monopoly for the East India Company
The Proclamation of 1763 banning western land claims

explanation: General search warrants called writs of assistance let British customs officers search any home or ship without probable cause.
fun_fact: James Otis argued against writs of assistance in 1761, inspiring John Adams to call it the spark of independence.

trap_notes.b: The Stamp Act involved taxation without representation, not search warrants.
trap_notes.c: The Tea Act involved trade monopolies, not home searches.
trap_notes.d: The Proclamation Line involved western settlement, not privacy.
trap_notes.default: The Fourth Amendment requires specific warrants based on probable cause.

prompt: Why did Congress create the Federal Reserve System in 1913 after the Panic of 1907?

options.text: To provide a central bank that stabilizes money and credit
To replace paper dollars with silver coins only
To abolish all private commercial banks nationwide
To give state governors control over tariff rates

explanation: In 1907, Wall Street had to rely on J.P. Morgan to rescue banks; Congress created the Fed in 1913 as a public lender of last resort.
fun_fact: The Federal Reserve Act set up 12 regional Reserve Banks so no single city controlled all U.S. credit.

trap_notes.b: The Fed created Federal Reserve notes as an elastic currency, not silver-only coins.
trap_notes.c: Private commercial banks remained the backbone of U.S. banking under Fed supervision.
trap_notes.d: Congress, not state governors, sets tariffs; the Fed manages monetary policy.
trap_notes.default: The Fed was built to prevent bank panics and manage the nation's money supply.

prompt: What made the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act a turning point in U.S. immigration law?

options.text: It was the first federal ban targeting a specific nationality
It granted automatic U.S. citizenship to all railroad workers
It lifted all limits on immigration from East Asia
It required European immigrants to enter via San Francisco

explanation: Passed amid West Coast labor resentment after the railroads were built, it barred Chinese laborers and blocked naturalization.
fun_fact: Congress did not repeal the Chinese Exclusion Act until 1943, when China was a U.S. ally in World War II.

trap_notes.b: The law actually barred Chinese immigrants from becoming U.S. citizens.
trap_notes.c: It imposed strict exclusion rather than lifting limits.
trap_notes.d: European immigrants mainly entered through East Coast ports like Ellis Island.
trap_notes.default: The 1882 act was the first major U.S. immigration law excluding a group by nationality.

prompt: What constitutional rule did United States v. Nixon (1974) establish during the Watergate scandal?

options.text: Executive privilege cannot shield evidence in a criminal trial
A president may ignore subpoenas from federal courts
Only the House Speaker can review White House tapes
Presidents are immune from all constitutional limits

explanation: A unanimous Supreme Court ordered Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes, affirming that no president is above the law.
fun_fact: Sixteen days after the Supreme Court ruling, Richard Nixon became the only U.S. president to resign.

trap_notes.b: The Court ruled that Nixon had to obey the federal subpoena.
trap_notes.c: The federal district court subpoenaed the tapes for a criminal trial.
trap_notes.d: The ruling reinforced the rule of law and limits on presidential power.
trap_notes.default: United States v. Nixon limited executive privilege and upheld the rule of law.

prompt: How did the Columbian Exchange reshape both the Americas and Europe after 1492?

options.text: Crops like potatoes fed Europe while diseases devastated Natives
Horses and cattle originated in North America before 1492
Corn and tomatoes came from Europe to the Americas
Trade between the hemispheres stayed limited to gold only

explanation: New World crops like potatoes and maize boosted Old World populations, while Old World diseases like smallpox ravaged Native peoples.
fun_fact: Horses brought by Spanish explorers transformed life for Plains Native nations within a few generations.

trap_notes.b: Modern horses and cattle were brought from Europe to the Americas after 1492.
trap_notes.c: Corn and tomatoes were native to the Americas and spread to Europe.
trap_notes.d: Plants, animals, people, and diseases all crossed the Atlantic in both directions.
trap_notes.default: Remember: potatoes and corn went east; horses, cattle, and smallpox went west.

prompt: Under British mercantilism, what role were the 13 colonies expected to play in the empire?

options.text: Supply raw materials and buy British manufactured goods
Trade freely with France and Spain on Dutch ships
Outlaw British imports to protect colonial factories
Mint their own gold coins to replace the British pound

explanation: The Navigation Acts required colonies to ship key raw goods like tobacco to Britain and buy finished goods from British merchants.
fun_fact: Until 1763, Britain practiced 'salutary neglect,' loosely enforcing trade rules while colonies prospered.

trap_notes.b: The Navigation Acts barred using foreign ships for key colonial exports.
trap_notes.c: Britain discouraged colonial manufacturing that competed with British workshops.
trap_notes.d: Britain restricted colonial currency rather than encouraging rival gold coins.
trap_notes.default: Mercantilism treated colonies as raw-material suppliers and captive markets for the mother country.

prompt: How did the 17th Amendment (1913) make the U.S. Senate more democratic?

options.text: It shifted Senate elections from state legislatures to voters
It allowed the president to appoint all U.S. senators
It gave larger states more senators based on population
It lowered the national voting age from 21 to 18

explanation: Before 1913, state legislatures picked U.S. senators; the 17th Amendment gave voters the power to elect senators directly.
fun_fact: Progressive reformers pushed the 17th Amendment after bribery scandals in state-level Senate elections.

trap_notes.b: Senators are elected by voters in each state, not appointed by the president.
trap_notes.c: Every state still gets exactly two senators regardless of population.
trap_notes.d: Lowering the voting age to 18 came later in the 26th Amendment (1971).
trap_notes.default: The 17th Amendment created direct popular election of U.S. senators.

prompt: Why did U.S. Secretary of State John Hay propose the 1899 Open Door Policy in China?

options.text: To keep Chinese ports open to U.S. trade alongside Europe
To ban all American exports from entering East Asia
To divide China into exclusive U.S. colonies
To invite European powers to colonize California

explanation: Fearing European powers and Japan would carve China into closed trade zones, Hay urged equal trading rights for all nations.
fun_fact: Acquiring the Philippines in 1898 gave U.S. merchants a Pacific stepping-stone toward Chinese markets.

trap_notes.b: The U.S. wanted to expand trade with China, not ban it.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. opposed closed spheres of influence so it could trade everywhere in China.
trap_notes.d: The Open Door Policy concerned trade in China, not California.
trap_notes.default: The Open Door Policy aimed to preserve equal U.S. commercial access in China.

prompt: What core supply-side idea guided President Reagan's 1981 tax and regulatory policies?

options.text: Cutting tax rates and rules spurs business investment
Raising top income taxes funds New Deal job agencies
Price controls and rationing curb consumer demand
Public ownership of airlines lowers ticket prices

explanation: Supply-side economics held that lower marginal tax rates and deregulation would boost investment, production, and jobs.
fun_fact: Combined with higher defense spending, the 1981 tax cuts also tripled the federal budget deficit during the 1980s.

trap_notes.b: Reagan cut the top income tax rate rather than raising it.
trap_notes.c: Nixon briefly used price controls in 1971; Reagan favored free-market deregulation.
trap_notes.d: Airlines and trucking were deregulated, not taken over by the government.
trap_notes.default: Reaganomics paired lower tax rates and deregulation to stimulate business supply.

prompt: How did Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) and the 1969 Cuyahoga River fire reshape U.S. policy?

options.text: They spurred creation of the EPA and Clean Water Act
They led Congress to abolish all national parks
They ended federal limits on industrial chemical waste
They sparked the 1933 Tennessee Valley dam project

explanation: Public alarm over DDT pesticides and burning polluted rivers led to Earth Day, the EPA (1970), and the Clean Water Act (1972).
fun_fact: Roughly 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day in April 1970.

trap_notes.b: Environmental laws expanded conservation rather than closing parks.
trap_notes.c: The EPA and Clean Water Act increased limits on industrial pollution.
trap_notes.d: The TVA began in 1933, nearly 30 years before Silent Spring.
trap_notes.default: 1960s environmental warnings directly produced the EPA and federal clean air and water laws.

prompt: Why is the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 viewed as the Articles of Confederation's lasting success?

options.text: It set a clear path for territories to join as equal states
It created a national Supreme Court and president
It expanded slavery across all Great Lakes territories
It gave Congress power to levy direct income taxes

explanation: The Northwest Ordinance banned slavery in the Northwest Territory, funded public schools, and let territories become equal states.
fun_fact: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin all entered the Union under the Northwest Ordinance's rules.

trap_notes.b: The U.S. Constitution, not the Northwest Ordinance, created the president and Supreme Court.
trap_notes.c: The Northwest Ordinance actually prohibited slavery north of the Ohio River.
trap_notes.d: Direct income taxes came much later under the 16th Amendment (1913).
trap_notes.default: The Northwest Ordinance created the orderly process for adding new states on equal footing.

prompt: How did Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika reforms affect U.S.-Soviet relations?

options.text: They eased tensions, led to arms cuts, and ended Soviet rule
They sparked the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis
They strengthened Soviet control over the Berlin Wall
They launched the Korean War along the 38th Parallel

explanation: Gorbachev's openness and economic reforms reduced Cold War hostility, leading to the 1987 INF Treaty and the 1991 Soviet breakup.
fun_fact: East and West Berliners tore down the Berlin Wall in November 1989 after Gorbachev refused to use Soviet troops.

trap_notes.b: The Cuban Missile Crisis happened in 1962 under Khrushchev and Kennedy.
trap_notes.c: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 during Gorbachev's reforms.
trap_notes.d: The Korean War began in 1950 under Joseph Stalin.
trap_notes.default: Gorbachev's 1980s reforms helped end the Cold War peacefully.

prompt: Why did Gilded Age factory owners support high protective tariffs while Midwest farmers opposed them?

options.text: Tariffs shielded U.S. mills while raising farm tool prices
Tariffs lowered prices on imported European steel
Tariffs paid direct cash subsidies to wheat growers
Tariffs banned U.S. factories from selling goods at home

explanation: High tariffs raised prices on foreign goods, helping U.S. factories while forcing farmers to pay more for tools.
fun_fact: Tariff debates were one of the fiercest partisan divides between Republicans and Democrats in the 1880s and 1890s.

trap_notes.b: Tariffs raised import prices rather than lowering them.
trap_notes.c: Tariffs taxed imports and did not pay cash subsidies to farmers.
trap_notes.d: Tariffs protected U.S. factories inside the domestic market.
trap_notes.default: Protective tariffs help domestic manufacturers charge higher prices, which hurts farm buyers.

prompt: What constitutional clash lay at the heart of the 1832–1833 Nullification Crisis?

options.text: Whether a state could declare a federal tariff law void
Whether Congress could pass a national income tax
Whether the president could serve more than two terms
Whether territories could vote in presidential elections

explanation: South Carolina claimed states could nullify the 1828 and 1832 tariffs, but President Jackson insisted federal law is supreme.
fun_fact: Henry Clay brokered a compromise tariff in 1833 that lowered rates while Congress passed the Force Bill.

trap_notes.b: Federal income taxes came much later in 1913 under the 16th Amendment.
trap_notes.c: Presidential term limits were set by the 22nd Amendment in 1951.
trap_notes.d: Territories still do not cast electoral votes in presidential elections.
trap_notes.default: Nullification tested whether state sovereignty could override federal law.

prompt: Why did critics mock the 1867 Alaska Purchase before gold, oil, and Cold War geography proved its value?

options.text: They saw a remote frozen land as 'Seward's Folly'
They feared Alaska was too densely populated to govern
They wanted Spain to keep Alaska as a buffer colony
They believed Alaska had no Pacific coastline at all

explanation: Critics mocked Seward for spending $7.2 million on ice, until gold, oil, and Arctic defense proved Alaska's value.
fun_fact: The U.S. bought Alaska from Russia for roughly two cents per acre.

trap_notes.b: Alaska was sparsely populated, not overcrowded.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. bought Alaska from Russia, not Spain.
trap_notes.d: Alaska has the longest coastline of any U.S. state.
trap_notes.default: Critics called it 'Seward's Folly' before its resources and strategic location paid off.

prompt: What Vietnam-era argument led to the rapid 1971 ratification of the 26th Amendment?

options.text: If 18-year-olds could be drafted to fight, they should vote
Only property owners over age 21 understood foreign policy
Poll taxes were needed to fund local high schools
States wanted to raise the minimum voting age to 25

explanation: With 18-year-olds drafted for Vietnam, states quickly ratified the 26th Amendment to lower the voting age to 18.
fun_fact: The 26th Amendment was ratified in just 100 days, the fastest amendment ratification in U.S. history.

trap_notes.b: The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18 and expanded the electorate.
trap_notes.c: The 24th Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
trap_notes.d: The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
trap_notes.default: Drafting 18-year-olds for Vietnam drove support for lowering the voting age to 18.
